title: Two services, and the pom.xml problem
goal: Copy the service, feel the duplication, then fix it with a multi-module build. Multi-module Maven makes no sense until you have something to share — now you do.
startWith: Step 03 finished: account-service is complete and its tests pass.

newIdeas.plain: A pom.xml with <packaging>pom</packaging> that produces no jar. Its job is to list <modules> and hold shared settings so one mvn install at the root builds everything in dependency order.
Tells a child pom where its parent is on disk. <relativePath>../../pom.xml</relativePath> means "two folders up". An empty <relativePath/> means the opposite: do not look on disk, download it.

A section in the root pom that says "if any module uses this library, here is the version" — without adding the dependency itself. Modules then declare dependencies with no version, and versions stay in one file.

-pl services/ledger-service means "build only this module". -am (also make) adds the modules it depends on. Without -am you build against the last jar you installed, which may be stale — and the failure looks like your code is wrong.

A shared module should hold data types and contracts — ids, money, event records. The moment business logic goes in there, every service must be redeployed to change it, and you have built a distributed monolith with extra steps.

tasks.do: Move account-service into a repository root and copy it to ledger-service
tasks.why: Copying is the fastest way to see what is genuinely shared. You cannot design a shared library from imagination.
tasks.how: This is a mechanical rename, and the part people get wrong is that Java package names are also folder names — a search-and-replace inside files is not enough. The script below moves the folders first, then rewrites the text, then renames the two application classes.

blocks.label: Create the repository root and move the finished service into it
blocks.body:
cd ..                                  # the folder that contains account-service/
mkdir -p ledgerflow/services ledgerflow/libs
mv account-service ledgerflow/services/account-service
mv infra ledgerflow/infra 2>/dev/null || true
cd ledgerflow                          # every command from now on runs from here

blocks.label: Copy it, then rename package folders as well as file contents
blocks.body:
cp -r services/account-service services/ledger-service
cd services/ledger-service

# 1. package names are folder names - move them first
mv src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/account src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger
mv src/test/java/io/ledgerflow/account src/test/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger

# 2. now rewrite what is inside the files
grep -rl 'account\|Account' src pom.xml \
  | xargs sed -i 's/io\.ledgerflow\.account/io.ledgerflow.ledger/g; s/Account/Ledger/g; s/account-service/ledger-service/g; s/account/ledger/g'

# 3. rename the classes whose names contained the old service name
mv src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/AccountServiceApplication.java \
   src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/LedgerServiceApplication.java 2>/dev/null || true
for f in $(find src -name 'Account*.java'); do mv "$f" "$(echo $f | sed 's/Account/Ledger/')"; done

cd ../..

blocks.label: Give it its own port and its own database
blocks.body:
# services/ledger-service/src/main/resources/application.yml
server:
  port: 8081
spring:
  application:
    name: ledger-service
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/ledger   # its own database, always

check.expect: 'clean'. Any leftover is a compile error waiting to happen.

tasks.do: Delete everything ledger does not own
tasks.why: A copied service arrives owning someone else's tables. Two services writing the same rows is the single worst mistake in this whole subject.
tasks.how: Ledger holds wallets; it does not own accounts. Delete the account code and the copied migrations, and write ledger's own baseline. Note the migration is V1__ again — Flyway version numbers are per database, and ledger has its own.

blocks.label: Remove the inherited account code and migrations
blocks.body:
cd services/ledger-service
rm -rf src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/adapter/in/web/AccountController.java \
       src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/adapter/out/persistence/*Entity.java \
       src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/adapter/out/persistence/Jpa*.java \
       src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/adapter/out/persistence/*Adapter.java \
       src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/application/AccountRepository.java \
       src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/domain/model/Account*.java \
       src/main/resources/db/migration/*.sql
rm -rf src/test/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/adapter src/test/java/io/ledgerflow/ledger/domain
cd ../..

blocks.label: services/ledger-service/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__holds.sql
blocks.body:
cat > services/ledger-service/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__holds.sql << 'EOF'
CREATE TABLE funds_holds (
    id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id    UUID         NOT NULL,
    wallet_code  VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,
    status      VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,      -- HELD | RELEASED | SOLD
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    expires_at  TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (account_id, wallet_code, status)
);
EOF

check.expect: Only V1__holds.sql. No accounts table anywhere in ledger.

tasks.why: One command should build the whole system, in the right order, with one set of versions.
tasks.how: It lives at the repository root, produces no jar, and lists the modules. Everything shared goes here: Java version, and the version numbers of any library more than one module uses.

blocks.label: ledgerflow/pom.xml
blocks.body:
cat > pom.xml << 'EOF'
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.1.1</version>
    <relativePath/>
  </parent>

  <groupId>io.ledgerflow</groupId>
  <artifactId>ledgerflow</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>pom</packaging>            <!-- builds no jar of its own -->

  <properties>
    <java.version>25</java.version>
    <springdoc.version>3.0.3</springdoc.version>
  </properties>

  <modules>
    <module>libs/ledgerflow-events</module>
    <module>services/account-service</module>
    <module>services/ledger-service</module>
  </modules>

  <dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
      <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
        <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
        <version>${springdoc.version}</version>
      </dependency>
    </dependencies>
  </dependencyManagement>
</project>
EOF

tasks.do: Create libs/ledgerflow-events and move the duplicated types into it
tasks.why: WalletRef and Money are now defined twice. Two definitions of the same idea drift, and then two services disagree about what a wallet is.
tasks.how: The library holds types both sides must agree on and nothing else — no controllers, no repositories, no business rules. One line matters more than it looks: do not put spring-boot-maven-plugin in a library pom. That plugin repackages a jar into an executable one and relocates the classes, so dependent services compile fine and then throw ClassNotFoundException at runtime.

blocks.label: libs/ledgerflow-events/pom.xml
blocks.body:
mkdir -p libs/ledgerflow-events/src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/events
cat > libs/ledgerflow-events/pom.xml << 'EOF'
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <parent>
    <groupId>io.ledgerflow</groupId>
    <artifactId>ledgerflow</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <relativePath>../../pom.xml</relativePath>   <!-- two folders up -->
  </parent>

  <artifactId>ledgerflow-events</artifactId>

  <!-- NO spring-boot-maven-plugin here. It would repackage this jar and
       every service depending on it would fail with ClassNotFoundException. -->
</project>
EOF

blocks.label: libs/ledgerflow-events/src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/events/WalletRef.java
libs/ledgerflow-events/src/main/java/io/ledgerflow/events/Money.java

tasks.do: Point both service POMs at the root and depend on the library
tasks.why: Until the parent changes, each service is still an island that happens to sit in the same folder.
tasks.how: In each of the two service poms: replace the <parent> block, delete the now-inherited <groupId>, <version> and <properties>, and add the library dependency. Keep spring-boot-maven-plugin in the services — they do produce executable jars.

blocks.label: services/*/pom.xml — the top of the file becomes this
blocks.body:
<parent>
  <groupId>io.ledgerflow</groupId>
  <artifactId>ledgerflow</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <relativePath>../../pom.xml</relativePath>
</parent>

<artifactId>account-service</artifactId>
<!-- delete the old groupId, version and <properties>: inherited now -->

blocks.label: One Maven wrapper for the whole repository, at the root
blocks.body:
mv services/account-service/mvnw services/account-service/mvnw.cmd services/account-service/.mvn .
rm -rf services/ledger-service/mvnw services/ledger-service/mvnw.cmd services/ledger-service/.mvn

tasks.do: Build the whole tree from the root
tasks.why: If the modules are wired correctly this is one command. If they are not, you find out now rather than in step 12.
tasks.how: -T 1C builds modules in parallel, one thread per CPU core. Maven still respects dependency order, so the library is built before the services that need it.

blocks.label: One service plus the libraries it depends on
Confirm the shared library really is on the classpath

check.expect: Reactor summary lists three modules, all SUCCESS.

proof.expect: Three modules build from the root and the shared types exist exactly once.
proof.note: If a change to ledgerflow-events does not seem to reach a service, you forgot -am, or you are building from inside the service folder instead of the root.

doneWhen: The whole tree builds from the root, no type is defined twice, and ledger owns no account tables.

lessons.title: Maven tool window
lessons.teach: Two modules means a reactor. Open Maven to see the module tree, run a goal on one module, and hit reload after every pom.xml edit — half of "IntelliJ can't find the class" is an unreloaded reactor.
